newsitem.title: UK: Only small risk in Yeltsin surgery -DeBakey.
newsitem.headline: Only small risk in Yeltsin surgery -DeBakey.

text.p: Leading U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey said on Wednesday there was only about a two to four percent risk involved in Russian President Boris Yeltsin's planned heart surgery.
"I think the risk is about the normal risk under these circumstances, which is not very high. It's maybe two, three, four percent," he said in an interview with British Broadcasting Corp radio.
DeBakey, a consultant on the surgery, said Yeltsin should be able to resume normal duties within six weeks to two months if the operation succeeds.
"He should be able to have another 10 years of good work life," DeBakey added.
He said the 65-year-old Russian leader could undergo the surgery as early as next week.
"We're shooting for next week, but I can't be any more specific than that because we'll probably be meeting on Monday with the medical team and making that decision -- exact date."
DeBakey said most of Yeltsin's medical problems holding up the surgery had now been corrected. "So we're about ready to go."
Asked to detail the problems, he said: "The anaemia and the blood loss, and efforts to determine its source, the thyroid disfunction and the cardiac improvement."
DeBakey said the surgery would "probably require a minimum of three and probably four bypasses".

The surgery will be performed by Russian cardiologist Renat Akchurin, who trained under DeBakey. DeBakey, 88, maintains a full schedule of surgery and teaches at the Baylor College of Medicine in Houston.
Yeltsin had two heart attacks last year and is believed to have suffered a third before his re-election in July for a second four-year term at the helm of the world's largest country.
In Russia on Tuesday, the Kremlin began issuing what it said would be regular medical bulletins about Yeltsin's condition.

"From this week, the final stage of the preparation for President Boris Yeltsin's operation has begun. Various degrees of functional tests will be undertaken and there will be round-the-clock monitoring," the bulletin said.
"The main aim of the final stage of the preparation is to bring the patient to the peak of his current physical and physiological capabilities."
